context: Both diagrams have five vertices in exactly the same positions: 1 at the upper left, 3 at the lower left, 5 at the upper middle, 2 at the lower middle, and 4 on the right. The comparison isolates the effect of edge direction.
description: The undirected graph on the left, labeled “Edges have no direction,” has seven edges without arrowheads: 1–2, 1–3, 1–5, 2–3, 2–4, 2–5, and 4–5. Each edge connects its endpoints in both directions. For example, edge 1–5 allows travel from 1 to 5 and from 5 to 1.

The directed graph on the right, labeled “Edges have a direction,” has nine arrows, listed by starting vertex: 1→3, 2→1, 2→4, 2→5, 3→1, 3→2, 4→5, 5→1, and 5→4. Vertices 1 and 3 have arrows in both directions, as do 4 and 5. Each of the other five connections has only one arrow.

frames.explanation: Opposite directed edges are independent. For example, the graph on the right has 5→1 but no direct edge 1→5. Vertex 1 can still reach 5 indirectly along 1→3→2→5. Direct travel both ways requires two oppositely directed edges. An indirect path does not count as a direct edge.
frames.title: Undirected and directed graphs: two-way connections and independent directed edges

summary: The same vertex layout uses plain lines and arrows to show how edge directions constrain travel.
title: Undirected and directed graphs: two-way connections and independent directed edges
